summary:
I've been building Keikochō, a Japanese-learning app for myself, and lately most of the interesting work has been on how grammar gets taught rather than what gets taught. Every grammar point had a short intro paragraph and drills, but I hadn't noticed the intros had crept from ~90 words to ~500 as I wrote later ones — the three chips I met first as a learner were the thinnest in the app. I split each one into a short primer plus a longer "study guide" block that only shows up on request, so the drill screen stays terse and the reference page can actually be a reference.

The harder half of that work was building guards that don't quietly stop meaning what they say. I had a test asserting every practice board was solvable from surface form alone — it stayed green for months while a dedupe bug meant 43% of one drill's answer choices were four copies of the correct one, because it deduped on an internal ID instead of the displayed text. Another guard checked a noun list against the lexicon but read the wrong JSON key, so it validated against an empty object and would have silently accepted "version" as a noun. Neither failure ever went red; both were only visible by rerunning the actual measurement the test was supposed to stand in for, not just the test suite. I've started writing that check explicitly into new guards: name the population a rate is measured over, and prove a negative assertion can actually fail before trusting it.

Also shipped: a "context" layer for the ~80 fixed phrases in the app (things like すみません or いらっしゃいませ) that previously had nothing but a one-line gloss. The rule I landed on — describe the situation a phrase is used in, never assert an etiquette verdict like "don't say this to your boss" — matters because a grammar claim can be checked against the app's own sentence data and a pragmatics claim can't be checked against anything I have.

Smaller thing, on the audio side: the text-to-speech engine I use reads Japanese through a real morphological analyzer, which occasionally refuses to synthesize a sentence because the reading is genuinely ambiguous — a word swallowing a neighboring particle in a way that changes its meaning. My first instinct was to patch around the refusal; the better rule turned out to be to trust it and treat every refusal as information about the language, not a bug in the pipeline.
